e.t: This adverb means “in herds,” describing animals or other creatures gathered and moving together as a group. It tells how something is done or how living creatures are arranged, rather than naming the creatures themselves. The word appears twice in the Greek LXX corpus, both times in 2 Maccabees. Its precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and sentence, but its central idea is collective movement or grouping like a herd.

This noun means “want of strength”: a lack of power or ability to act effectively. It describes weakness or insufficiency rather than strength itself. In the Greek Old Testament and related LXX corpus, it occurs twice, once in Amos and once in 3 Maccabees. Its basic sense is broad, so the surrounding verse shows whether the lack concerns a person, a group, or a situation. It is a straightforward term for being without sufficient strength.

This noun means “their nobles,” referring to people of elevated standing who belong to or are associated with a particular group. The possessive word “their” shows that these nobles are connected with others already understood from the surrounding passage. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs once, in Nehemiah 3:5. Its precise role there depends on the surrounding verse and passage, but its basic meaning is a group’s nobles.

This adjective describes someone or something regarded with reverence—worthy of honor, respect, or awe. It presents its subject as august, carrying a sense of dignity that calls forth respectful regard rather than casual treatment. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, both occurrences appearing in Ezekiel 23:20. The exact force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and its imagery, but the word itself points to what is treated as venerable or deserving reverence.

This verb means “take captive”: to seize people and make them captives. It describes an action carried out against people, whether the captors are taking individuals or a larger group. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs 14 times. Its use spans Old Testament and deuterocanonical books, so it consistently names the act of bringing people under captivity rather than simply overcoming them in battle.

This word is a proper name, rendered “Akchobōr” or “Akkhovor.” It functions as a specific name rather than a general description or action word. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Jeremiah 43:12. The available information identifies the name and its location, but does not provide enough surrounding verse text to explain whether it names a person, place, or another particular entity. Its precise significance therefore depends on the passage in which the name appears.

This Greek LXX noun means “that which is given.” It names the thing or offering that is given, rather than the act of giving itself. The word occurs 11 times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical corpus, so it describes a recurring idea rather than a rare expression. Its precise sense in any particular verse depends on what is being given in that passage.

This LXX word means “sinful.” It can describe a person or thing characterized by sin, functioning as either a noun or an adjective. Its basic sense points to moral wrongdoing rather than merely weakness, suffering, or ordinary imperfection. The word occurs 139 times in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented in this corpus, showing that it is a recurring description of those identified by sinful conduct. Its precise force in a particular verse depends on the surrounding context.

Amizabath is a personal name, also given as “Amizavath.” It identifies an individual rather than describing an action, quality, or object. This name appears once in the Greek Old Testament, at 1 Chronicles 27:6. Because the available material provides the name but no further word meaning or verse text, its significance here is limited to identifying that person. Its precise role in the verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This adjective describes someone or something that is “without share in”—not having a part, portion, or participation in something. It expresses exclusion from what others possess or experience, while the surrounding sentence identifies what is lacking. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs once, in Wisdom 2:9. Its precise force there depends on the wording and context of that passage.

This Greek Old Testament noun means “outlay” or “expenditure”—the spending or using up of resources. It describes a cost that is paid or incurred, rather than an object, person, or action by itself. The word occurs four times in the Greek Old Testament, in Deuteronomy and Ezekiel. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on what is being spent and the surrounding sentence, but its central idea remains the expense or consumption of something valuable.

This noun means “wind-blast,” referring to a forceful movement or burst of wind. It names a natural phenomenon rather than an action or person. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs three times, in Deuteronomy, 2 Chronicles, and Haggai. Its precise force in any one passage depends on the surrounding verse, but the basic idea remains a blast of wind. The word does not itself specify whether the wind is gentle or damaging; that must be determined from the context in which it appears.

This verb means “hold contrary tenets,” describing the act of maintaining beliefs or teachings that oppose a stated position. It presents a person as taking an opposing doctrinal or philosophical view, rather than merely expressing a passing disagreement. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, the word occurs once, in 4 Maccabees 8:15. Its precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and argument.

This noun means “inability to see”—the condition of being unable to perceive visually. It can describe blindness or a temporary loss of sight, while the surrounding passage determines how the condition functions in a particular verse. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs six times across five verses, including Genesis, Deuteronomy, 2 Kings, Wisdom, and 2 Maccabees. Its central idea remains the absence or loss of visual perception.

This LXX word means “all at once” or “everything.” It describes something viewed as complete, whole, or taken together rather than only part of it. As an adjective or noun, it can refer either to the whole of something or to all its members collectively. The word occurs 49 times in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented in this LXX corpus, showing regular use for totality and completeness. Its exact force in a particular verse depends on the noun or situation it describes.

This Greek LXX preposition means “from” or “away,” marking separation, movement out of a place, or the point from which something comes. It can describe leaving a location, being removed from something, or origin. The word appears 3,750 times in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented in this corpus, so it is a common connective word whose precise force depends on the sentence around it. Its central idea remains distance or source: something comes from somewhere or moves away from it.

Arabissa, also rendered Aravissa, is a proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or relationship. It identifies a specific named entity in the Greek Old Testament tradition and occurs once, in Job 42:17. Because the available material does not include the verse text or surrounding context, its precise role in that passage cannot be explained further here. The name itself is preserved as Arabissa or Aravissa.

This noun means “booty” or “prey”—something seized, taken, or held as the result of taking from others. It can describe property captured or people treated as vulnerable objects of seizure. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek Jewish writings represented here, it occurs 17 times, showing a recurring concern with what is unjustly taken and with the release or protection of those treated as prey. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage.

Asaph is a proper name, rendered “Asaph” or “Asaf.” It identifies a person rather than expressing an action, quality, or ordinary object. In the Greek Old Testament, this name occurs 44 times across 39 verses, especially in 1 Chronicles, Psalms, and related historical records. The name appears in passages concerning named individuals, so its precise reference depends on the surrounding passage. It should therefore be read as a personal designation, not as a general word with several unrelated meanings.

This adjective means discordant: it describes something that does not agree, blend, or sound harmonious with something else. It can describe disagreement or a lack of harmony, whether in sound, words, or related things. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, the word occurs twice, in Wisdom 18:10 and Bel and the Dragon 1:15. Its exact force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and subject being described.

Achima, also rendered Akhima, is a proper name—the personal name of an individual rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at Joshua 15:14. The name identifies a person, but without the verse text, that person’s role or the significance of the name cannot be stated reliably. Its meaning is therefore best represented simply as the personal name “Achima” or “Akhima.”

Achitōb, also rendered Akhitov, is a personal name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it identifies particular people in Israel’s history. The name occurs 14 times across 14 verses, appearing in 1 Samuel, 2 Samuel, 1 Chronicles, and Ezra. Its precise reference depends on the surrounding passage, since the same name is used in more than one historical setting.

Basa is a proper name, also rendered “Vasa.” It identifies a named person or place rather than describing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Greek Old Testament, this name occurs once, at 1 Kings 2:46. The available information identifies the name itself but does not provide enough surrounding verse text to specify whether Basa refers to a person or a location in that passage.

This noun means “mire,” referring to muddy ground in which movement may be difficult. It names a physical condition rather than an action, person, or quality. In the Greek Old Testament corpus, it occurs twice, both within one verse of Jeremiah: Jeremiah 45:6. The available word information identifies its central meaning but does not include the verse text, so the precise force of the word in that passage must be understood from its surrounding context.

Galgal is a proper name, preserved in English as “Galgal.” It identifies a named location or landmark rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs nine times across nine verses, especially in Joshua, Judges, and the prophets. Because the available wording gives the name but not the surrounding verse text, its particular significance must be understood from the passage where it appears.

This verb means to load something or fill it up. It describes putting contents into a container, vehicle, or other space until it is filled or sufficiently supplied. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs twice: once in Genesis and once in 3 Maccabees. Its exact force in either passage depends on what is being filled and the surrounding sentence, but the central idea remains the act of loading or filling.

This word is a personal name, rendered “Gouni” or “Guni.” It identifies an individual rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs once, at 1 Chronicles 5:15. Because the verse text and surrounding passage are not included here, the name itself can be explained clearly, but the person’s specific role in that passage must be understood from the biblical context.

This word is a proper name, rendered as “Dalia” or “Thalia.” It identifies a person rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament (LXX) corpus, it occurs once, in 1 Chronicles 4:19. The surrounding verse text is not available here, so the name itself can be explained, but the person’s precise role in that passage cannot be stated from this word alone.

This noun refers to a “second rate” or a “retelling”—something presented again or in a secondary form. It can describe a repeated account or a subsequent version rather than the original presentation. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings, it occurs three times: twice in 2 Kings and once in Sirach. The surrounding passage determines whether the emphasis is on a second arrangement, a repeated account, or another secondary presentation.

This Greek verb means to “spar with” or “skirmish with.” It describes an active clash or struggle between people rather than a quiet disagreement. As a verb, it expresses what someone does when engaging another person in a contest or hostile exchange. In the Greek Old Testament, this word occurs once, in Exodus 2:13. The precise force of the action in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but the word itself centers on opposing or contending with someone.

This verb means “thoroughly keep; maintain.” It describes preserving or continuing to hold something carefully, rather than abandoning or losing it. The word can describe an ongoing responsibility to keep what has been entrusted, commanded, or established. In the Greek Old Testament and deuterocanonical books, it occurs 23 times, showing a repeated sense of sustained keeping across different settings. Its precise force in a particular verse depends on what is being preserved and the surrounding context.

This verb means to “thoroughly/fully interpret”—to explain or make the meaning of something clear in a complete way. It describes an act of interpretation rather than a person, object, or quality. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 2 Maccabees 1:36. The surrounding verse text is not available, so the word’s precise force in that sentence must be understood from its context. Its central idea remains careful, complete interpretation.

This noun means a donation: something given or presented to another person. It describes the act or thing given, whether offered as help, honor, or support. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs 21 times, including uses in Genesis, Proverbs, and Sirach. Its precise emphasis in any verse depends on what is being given and why, but the central idea remains a freely given gift or contribution.

Dōdō, also rendered Thotho, is a proper name identifying a person rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at 1 Chronicles 11:26. Because personal names generally identify individuals rather than express a broader idea, its meaning here is primarily the person’s name. The surrounding verse would be needed to explain that individual’s role or significance in the passage.

This Greek LXX verb means “give.” It expresses the action of giving and may describe what someone does toward another person or situation. The word appears eight times across seven verses in the LXX corpus, in Proverbs and Sirach. Its exact force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central meaning remains the act of giving. It is distinct here as a Greek LXX word, so its meaning is being described within that Greek Old Testament and related wisdom-text setting.

This Greek verb means “speak out”: to express something openly in words rather than keep it unspoken. It describes an action of verbal expression, not a person, object, or quality. In the Greek Old Testament corpus represented here, it occurs once, in Sirach 19:25. Its precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and argument, but its basic sense remains the act of speaking out or making something known aloud.

Elzabad is a personal name, rendered “Elzabad; Elzavath.” It identifies an individual rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Greek Old Testament, this name occurs once, at 1 Chronicles 26:7. Since it is a proper name, its main function is to distinguish this person from others mentioned in the passage. The name itself should therefore be understood as a personal designation, while the surrounding verse supplies the person’s specific role or connection.

This adjective means “Greek” or describes “Greek customs.” It identifies something associated with Greek people, culture, or practices, depending on the sentence in which it appears. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs eight times, including passages in Jeremiah, 2 Maccabees, and 4 Maccabees. The word itself describes a cultural or customary connection rather than naming a person or action. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on what thing, practice, or group it modifies.

This adjective describes something positioned at the fore or at the front. It refers to a location or part that is ahead of, or facing before, something else. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs two times, in Exodus and 2 Maccabees, showing a limited but consistent positional meaning. Its precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding context, but its central idea remains placement toward the front.

This word means “nine,” the number that comes after eight and before ten. It is an indeclinable number word, so it identifies a quantity rather than an action, person, or quality. In the LXX corpus, it occurs 34 times, appearing in statements about ages, counts, and numbered offerings or groups. Its exact reference—whether a person’s age, a census total, or another count—comes from the surrounding verse.

This adjective means “sixty years old.” It describes someone or something by stating an age of sixty years, functioning as an age description rather than naming a person or action. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, both times in Leviticus 27. Its precise force in either verse depends on the surrounding wording, but its basic meaning remains a clear reference to being sixty years old.

This adverb means “afterward,” referring to something that happens later in a sequence or after an earlier event. It helps connect one action, statement, or stage with what follows, showing that the second comes afterward rather than at the same time. In the Greek Old Testament corpus, it occurs two times: once in Isaiah and once in 4 Maccabees. Its exact force in either passage depends on the surrounding sentence and the events being connected.

gl: one who presses on a work
d: one who presses on a work

e.t: This noun refers to “one who presses on a work”—a person who applies himself energetically and persistently to a task. Its wording emphasizes active effort directed toward completing or advancing work, rather than merely observing or beginning it. In the Greek Old Testament, this word occurs once, in Isaiah 14:4. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic sense describes someone earnestly pressing forward in labor.

gl: coupled with an animal of diverse kind
d: coupled with an animal of diverse kind

e.t: This adjective describes being coupled with an animal of a different kind. It refers to a pairing in which the two animals are not the same kind, rather than simply describing any ordinary partnership. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Leviticus 19:19. The precise force of the word in that verse depends on the surrounding command, but its direct meaning is a coupling involving unlike kinds of animals.

This word describes someone hostile or refers to an enemy—one who stands opposed to another. As an adjective, it marks hostility; as a noun, it identifies an opponent or enemy. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs 425 times, showing that it is a regular word for personal or opposing enemies. Its range includes enemies faced by individuals, communities, and Israel. The surrounding passage determines who is hostile and what opposition is involved.

Zoue, also rendered Zue, is a proper name referring to a person rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at 1 Chronicles 5:13. Because the verse text and surrounding passage are not included here, the name itself identifies the individual, while the surrounding biblical context supplies any further information about that person.

This Greek LXX verb means “produce life” or “make live.” It describes the action of bringing something into life or preserving it so that it lives. As a verb, it expresses an act rather than naming a person, object, or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs 11 times across 10 verses, including passages in Exodus, Leviticus, Judges, 1 Samuel, 1 Kings, and 2 Kings. Its exact force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage.

Thaesthen is a proper name in the Greek Old Testament, preserved as a name rather than translated into an ordinary descriptive term. Its supplied meaning is simply “Thaesthen.” It occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, at 2 Kings 19:12. Without the verse text or surrounding context, the available information does not establish whether the name refers to a person, place, or another named entity. Its role and significance therefore depend on the passage where it appears.

This adjective describes something wonderful or speaks of wonders—things that inspire awe and admiration. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it is used for remarkable acts or things worthy of wonder. The word occurs 56 times, with many occurrences in Psalms, and is rendered “wonderful” and “wonders.” Its exact force in any verse depends on what remarkable thing the surrounding passage is describing.

This verb means to furnish something with doors or to shut it close. It describes the act of securing an opening by adding or closing a door, rather than referring to the door itself. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs once, in 1 Maccabees 4:57. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic sense remains the enclosing or securing of a place with doors.

Iamini is a proper name, referring to a person rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Greek Old Testament, this name occurs twice, both times in Numbers 26. The name itself identifies the person, while the surrounding verse and passage provide any further information about that individual. Its meaning should therefore be understood primarily as a personal designation, not as a descriptive word with a broader everyday definition.

Ieramēli, also rendered Ieramili, is a personal name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it identifies a particular person or family connection. This name occurs once, in 1 Samuel 30:29, and its precise reference there depends on the surrounding verse and passage. The name itself does not provide a broader concept or teaching apart from identifying the person to whom it refers.

This adjective describes someone or something bold in a reckless, daring way. It points to confidence that is not restrained by caution, so the emphasis is not simply courage but audacity that may disregard danger or consequences. The word occurs twice in the Greek Old Testament, both times in Jeremiah. Its exact force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and description, but its central idea remains boldness marked by recklessness.

This verb means “come far behind”: it describes a person or thing that does not keep pace and is left well behind. As a verb, it expresses an action or condition of falling seriously behind rather than merely being slightly delayed. In the LXX corpus, including its Old Testament and deuterocanonical writings, it occurs four times. Its ordinary sense is clear, while its precise force in any passage depends on the surrounding words.

This word means “that one too,” referring to another person or thing while adding it to what has already been mentioned. It combines a pointing idea—“that one”—with an additional idea—“too.” As a pronoun joined with a conjunction, it helps connect someone or something with a previous subject. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs four times, including three occurrences in Isaiah and one in Wisdom. Its precise reference in any passage depends on the surrounding sentence.

This Greek LXX verb means “hunt down; drive hard,” describing determined pursuit that presses after someone or forces them onward. It can refer to pursuing people in conflict or driving them vigorously, while the surrounding passage determines the precise force. The word occurs 85 times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical writings, from Genesis through 1 Maccabees, showing that it is used repeatedly for forceful pursuit rather than a single isolated action.

In the Greek LXX, this noun means “catastrophe”: a disastrous event marked by serious ruin or upheaval. It names the calamity itself rather than a person, action, or quality. The word occurs 16 times across the LXX corpus, including both Old Testament and deuterocanonical books, so it can describe a repeated scriptural category of severe destruction. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage.

Kedmōnaios, also rendered Kethmoneos, is a proper name in the Greek Old Testament. It identifies a named entity rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. The form appears once in the Greek translation of the Old Testament, at Genesis 15:19. Because it is a proper name and no broader definition is supplied, its main meaning is the name itself; the surrounding verse provides the specific identification intended there.

This Greek LXX noun means “branch,” referring to a woody limb growing from a tree or plant. It is used for branches in descriptions of trees and their spreading growth. The word occurs 27 times in the Greek LXX corpus, appearing in both the Old Testament and deuterocanonical books. Its exact force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning remains a branch or bough.

This Greek noun means “companion”—a person who is associated with another or shares company with them. It describes someone connected as a fellow participant, associate, or partner in a relationship or activity. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs eight times, including passages from Kings, Esther, Isaiah, Malachi, and Sirach. The surrounding verse determines whether the word points to a close companion, an associate, or another person joined in a shared setting.

This word means “gourd,” referring to a plant that can provide shade or shelter. It is a noun used in the Greek Old Testament, appearing five times across four verses, all within Jonah 4. The word is repeated in the passage’s account of the gourd’s growth, its destruction, and Jonah’s concern over it. Its basic meaning identifies the plant itself; the surrounding passage determines the larger significance of what happens to it.

This noun means “crocus,” the name of a flowering plant. It identifies the plant itself rather than an action, quality, or person. In the Greek Old Testament, the word occurs twice: once in Proverbs and once in Song of Songs. The references are Proverbs 7:17 and Song of Songs 4:14. Its precise significance in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and passage, but its basic meaning remains the name of the crocus flower.

This Greek LXX verb means “blossom,” describing the action of coming into bloom. It is used twice, both times in Song of Songs chapter 2. As a verb, it presents blossoming as an action or development rather than as a flower or plant itself. Its precise force in either verse depends on the surrounding wording, but its central meaning remains the appearance or growth of a blossom.

This word is a personal name, referring to a person rather than describing an action, quality, or object. It is rendered “Labanō; Lavano,” showing that its role is to identify an individual. In the Greek Old Testament (LXX), it occurs once, in Ezra 2:45. Because no verse text or surrounding context is provided here, the name itself does not establish anything further about the person or the passage. Its meaning is therefore chiefly identificational: it functions as a proper name.

This Greek LXX noun means “forgetfulness”: the condition of failing to remember or losing something from memory. It names an absence or lapse of remembrance rather than an action someone performs. The word occurs 11 times in the Greek LXX corpus, appearing in both the Old Testament and deuterocanonical books. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic sense remains the loss or absence of memory.

Magadagad is a proper name, also rendered Magathagath. It identifies a named location or entity in the Greek Old Testament, but the available wording does not provide a further definition of the name itself. This word occurs once in the Greek Septuagint, in Joshua 15:37. Its precise significance there depends on the surrounding verse and list of names, but lexically it functions as a name rather than as a description or action.

This LXX word means “from far,” describing something viewed, heard, approached, or situated at a distance from a person or place. It functions as an adverb or preposition, so it normally tells where an action occurs or from what distance someone observes or comes. It appears 33 times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books, including passages in Genesis, Exodus, Joshua, and 1 Samuel. The exact force in any verse comes from the surrounding sentence, but its central idea remains distance: from a far-off place or position.

ματαιόω means “superficial.” As a verb, it describes becoming or making something superficial rather than deep or substantial. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears six times in six verses, across several books. Its precise role depends on the sentence: it may describe what someone does or the condition that results. The surrounding verse is needed to determine how this basic idea functions in each occurrence.

This noun refers to great boasting or arrogance—an inflated, self-important attitude expressed through proud claims or behavior. It describes more than ordinary confidence: the emphasis is on excessive self-exaltation. In the Greek Old Testament corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 4 Maccabees 2:15. The exact force of the word in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central meaning is clear: boastful pride that elevates oneself beyond what is fitting.

This adjective means “monthly,” describing something that takes place or is arranged once each month. It identifies a regular time pattern rather than a person, object, or action by itself. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs ten times, all in Leviticus and Numbers, where the surrounding passages determine what is being counted, assigned, or regulated on that monthly schedule. Its basic meaning remains straightforward: it marks a connection with a month or a recurring monthly interval.

This word means “calf,” referring to a young bovine animal. It is a noun used for an animal in the Greek Old Testament, including calves presented in worship, kept among herds, or made into an image. Its basic meaning remains the same wherever it appears; the surrounding passage determines the particular role of the calf in that verse. The word occurs 227 times in the Greek Old Testament, with especially frequent use in Numbers and Leviticus.

This Greek LXX adjective means “intellectual,” describing something connected with the mind, understanding, or thought. It functions as a descriptive word rather than naming a person or action by itself. In the Wisdom of Solomon, it occurs twice, in Wisdom 7:22 and 7:23, so its precise force in either verse depends on the noun or idea it describes there. The central sense remains mental or understanding-related, pointing readers toward the activity or quality of the mind.

This LXX word means “eight thousand.” It describes a quantity, functioning either as a number that identifies eight thousand or as a noun referring to that amount. It occurs 10 times in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek books represented here, from Numbers through 2 Maccabees. Its use includes counted groups and amounts, so its basic meaning remains precise and numerical rather than describing a person, quality, or action.

This Greek LXX verb means “appear” or “seen”: it describes someone or something becoming visible or being perceived. It is a verb, so it expresses an action or occurrence rather than naming a person, object, or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in 1 Kings 8:8. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic sense remains the act of appearing or being seen.

This verb means “make holy; purify.” It describes an action that sets something apart as holy or cleanses it for a holy purpose. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs three times: twice in Old Testament passages and once in Wisdom. The definition emphasizes the action of making holy or purifying rather than merely naming a holy state. The surrounding verse determines what is being made holy or purified.

This Greek LXX verb means “see” or “look.” It describes directing one’s sight toward something or becoming aware of what is before the eyes. In ordinary sentences, it can refer simply to visual attention, whether someone looks at something or sees it. The word occurs 19 times in the Greek Old Testament and related LXX writings, showing a recurring, straightforward use rather than a rare or specialized sense. Its exact force in a particular verse comes from the surrounding sentence.

This adjective means “absolute,” describing something as not partial or limited. It identifies the noun or idea it modifies as standing in an unrestricted, total way. The word occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, in 3 Maccabees 7:16. Its precise force there depends on the surrounding wording, but its central sense is a strong description of absoluteness rather than something qualified or divided.

This noun means “transgression”: a violation or crossing of a commanded boundary. It names the wrongful act itself rather than the person who commits it. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs three times—in Psalms, Wisdom, and 2 Maccabees. Its precise force in any one passage depends on the surrounding verse, but its central idea remains a breach of what is required or rightly established.

This noun means “falling beside,” presenting the idea of a person or thing falling or moving alongside rather than remaining in its proper place. As a noun, it names this kind of falling or departure. In the Greek Old Testament corpus, it occurs once, in Jeremiah 22:21. Its precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and context, but the central idea remains a falling beside or aside.

This word means “leopard,” the name of a swift, powerful wild animal. It is a noun used for the animal itself, whether mentioned as part of the created world or used in biblical imagery. In the Greek Old Testament corpus, it occurs eight times, including passages in Isaiah, Jeremiah, Daniel, Hosea, and Habakkuk. Its precise significance in any particular verse comes from the surrounding passage, but the word’s ordinary meaning remains the leopard as an animal.

e.h: A Residence or Place of Dwelling
e.t: This Greek LXX noun means “residence”: a place or condition where someone lives or stays. It refers to dwelling rather than to a person, action, or possession. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs five times, appearing in Genesis, Psalms, and Sirach. Its precise emphasis in any individual verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central idea remains a residence or period of dwelling.

This Greek noun means “chance,” referring to something that happens without being presented as the result of a deliberate plan. It names an occurrence or circumstance considered accidental or unforeseen rather than a person, action, or command. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears twice, once in Ruth and once in 2 Samuel. Its precise force in either verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic sense remains “chance.”

This Greek LXX verb means “blow,” describing the act of moving air by breath or wind. It presents blowing as an action rather than a thing or quality.
